# Florida Atlantic University — School of Architecture

## ARC 3133-001 — Architectural Visualization Methods 1

### Computational Visualization + Digital Fabrication

**Term:** Fall 2026 — Full Term · **Credits:** 3

**Meeting:** Tuesday, 5:00 PM–7:50 PM · **Location:** FAU/BC Higher Ed Complex FTL — room to be confirmed

**Instructors:**

## Course description

Use computational methods to build, vary and communicate architectural form. Each assignment asks you to explain what your system does and demonstrate it through a clear result.

P1 establishes graphic standards. P2 is procedural: transformations, Boolean operations and ordered instructions. P3 is parametric: descriptive geometry, lists, reusable modules, repetition, conditions and attractors. P4 is generative: systematic field exploration, an architectural envelope and a fabricated contour model.

Use real architectural precedents for CSG and module construction. In 3.5, reuse the existing panel to design an architectural application with attractors. Use your Graphic Standards Manual throughout. Plain-language explanations, readable drawings and useful parameter values matter more than formal mathematical notation on assignment sheets. Explained mathematics remains in the lessons and presentations.

Project 4 develops one pavilion or small shop within a maximum 12 x 12 x 12 m envelope. All new required instruction ends by Week 12. The contour model is due in Week 13; the remaining classes support feedback, revisions and booklet preparation.

## Learning outcomes

- Build a consistent design system through color, type, composition and templating.
- Interpret documented architecture using transformations, Boolean operations and clear instructions.
- Explain how slicer settings and print strategies affect a physical result.
- Construct a reusable module from points, edges, faces and lists, with meaningful parameter inputs.
- Use repetition, nesting, indices, modulo and conditions to organize architectural patterns.
- Use point and curve attractor fields to vary an existing panel and develop an architectural application.
- Build a two-parameter matrix with supplied generative-field tools, interpret the results and refine a selected architectural envelope.
- Prepare aligned contour parts, test their assembly and communicate a coherent physical model.

## Learning pace and class format

Attractors are taught October 20. Submit the 3.4 studies and 3.5 architectural application together on October 27. Each subsequent class introduces the next assignment, due one week later.

October 27: submit 3.4-3.5 and begin the student-built 5 x 5 matrix (4.1). November 3: submit 4.1 and begin the pavilion or small-shop envelope (4.2). November 10: submit 4.2 and begin contour fabrication (4.3). November 17: bring the physical contour model to class and submit its fabrication sheet and files.

Digital submissions are due at 11:59 PM Eastern Time on each due date. All new required content ends November 10 (Week 12). November 17 begins feedback on the completed project; November 24 and December 1 support revisions, documentation and booklet preparation. No new graded assignment is due December 1. The booklet and revised GSM remain due at the December 10-16 final review; the exact review slot will be announced.

The recorded midterm deadline remains October 18 at 11:59 PM Eastern Time on Teams for 1, 2.1, 2.2, 3.1 and 3.2. Review that work using the evidence already submitted; this schedule adds no retrospective deliverables or midterm assessment.

Each class is a short demonstration, then guided practice and critique. Start from a small example, check that it works, then make it more complex. Watch the video tutorial for the topic when one is posted.

Bring your editable file to every class. Be ready to change an input, predict what will happen and explain the nodes involved. Reviews look at both your visual work and your understanding of the process.

Plan for at least six hours of work outside class each week, including fabrication preparation, tests and documentation. Classes and scheduled FabLab work are in person.

## P1 — GSM

Build a standardized graphic system through color theory, typography, composition and your own reusable template.

<a id="gsm"></a>

### 1 — Graphic Standards Manual

**Introduced:** Week 1 — Aug 25 · **Due:** Sun Oct 18, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 5%

**Present:** Four 17 x 11 inch pages in one PDF: template, typography, color/line styles and an applied sheet; editable layout and assets.

- Make four pages: sheet grid and composition; typography; color and line styles; an applied course sheet.
- Use 17 x 11 inch landscape pages. Show useful settings beside examples, including margins, type sizes and line weights.
- Choose up to two colors plus a white or dark background. Give either HEX or RGB values and explain the palette relationship, such as complementary or analogous. If starting from a triad, identify the two hues you retained.
- Keep the type hierarchy simple: no more than three typefaces, four hierarchy levels and four line weights.
- Study the reference manuals in Resources, credit one useful idea, and test the system on your own work. Apply it to every assignment and the final booklet.

**Ungraded checkpoints:**

- Week 2 — Sep 1: Bring a sample sheet for an ungraded identity check.
- Final review — December 10–16, 2026; exact review slot to be confirmed: Submit the revised manual as a separate PDF alongside the booklet.

## P2 — CSG

Interpret real architecture through transformations and Boolean operations, explain it as instructions, then learn slicing and 3D printing.

<a id="p2a"></a>

### 2.1 — CSG - an architectural object as instructions

**Introduced:** Week 2 — Sep 1 · **Due:** Sun Oct 18, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 10%

**Present:** One 17 x 11 inch sheet: precedent, numbered diagrams/instructions and final view; editable model.

- Choose a documented real project. Credit the project, architect and image source; identify the main forms you will simplify.
- Build an editable model from basic solids and transformations. Demonstrate union, subtraction and intersection; a small supporting comparison is acceptable if one operation is unnecessary in the main object.
- Explain the construction in about six to nine diagram steps. Match each step to a short instruction in ordinary language; formal code is not required.
- Use BIG-style graphics: white building masses, restrained color for changes or operations, clear outlines and simple line weights. Show context or vegetation in the final view.
- Name or separate objects when it helps explain the sequence. Use the [BIG-style diagram tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Y5Rn3bDL5s) in Resources.

<a id="p2b"></a>

### 2.2 — 3D printing - from model to layers

**Introduced:** Week 3 — Sep 8 · **Due:** Sun Oct 18, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 5%

**Present:** One CSG print; photograph and annotated slicer documentation PDF; editable geometry, print mesh and slicer settings/project.

- Check units and size, choose an orientation and inspect the layer preview before printing.
- Use a strategy to avoid or reduce supports: reorient the object, separate it into parts or adjust overhangs. Bridging is acceptable when the test or preview supports it.
- Identify the settings that matter for your object: layer height, walls, infill, adhesion and supports. Explain your choices briefly rather than listing every software option.
- Keep the assembled object within 60 mm on each axis and within the existing 200 g filament allowance, including tests and failed attempts.
- Document a problem and response, or an anticipated problem checked in the preview. Follow the FabLab workflow.

**Ungraded checkpoints:**

- Week 6 — Sep 29: Before you queue the print, check the geometry, units, orientation and sliced preview.

## P3 — Paneling

Build a reusable module from a documented panel system. Use lists, repetition, conditions and attractors to develop architectural studies.

<a id="p3a"></a>

### 3.1 — Descriptive geometry - build a reusable module

**Introduced:** Week 4 — Sep 15 · **Due:** Sun Oct 18, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 10%

**Present:** One 17 x 11 inch sheet: panel precedent, three variations, indexed point/face lists and parameter table; editable module.

- Choose and credit a real panel or architectural system. Show enough reference material to explain your interpretation.
- Construct the panel using explicit points and faces that refer to those points. Show readable point and face lists; no separate explanation of face winding or normals is required.
- Expose a few meaningful parameters, such as width, opening or depth. Show three settings that reveal how the same module changes.
- Use one material and consistent three-point lighting for the comparison. The [lighting tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RDbrOpnIY7Q) is in Resources; no lighting diagram or material-settings table is required.
- Check that the module works when repeated. For a complex panel with 24 or more points, a Boolean may supplement the construction if at least 16 explicit points generate geometry; review this route with your professor.

<a id="p3b"></a>

### 3.2 — Arrays - repetition, patterns and architecture

**Introduced:** Week 6 — Sep 29 · **Due:** Sun Oct 18, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 10%

**Present:** Three 17 x 11 inch sheets in one PDF: four repetition diagrams, four conditional patterns and an architectural application; editable studies.

- 3.2.1 - Repetition: show the module alone, then in a 1D row, 2D grid and 3D array. Label counts and spacing. Identify how repetition is nested and what each index refers to.
- 3.2.2 - Conditional patterns: show four patterns on a consistent array. Include a modulo-based rule and an index-driven parameter change. Caption each with a simple rule such as "shift every other row" or "increase the opening along the row."
- 3.2.3 - Architectural application: combine the previous studies into one simple facade, wall, canopy, building or similar object. Show an overall view and a supporting view explaining the module and pattern.
- Reuse your module and one readable graphic setup. Describe the rules in ordinary language; formal equations, count products and polished lighting variations are not required.

<a id="p3study"></a>

### 3.4 — Attractors - three field studies

**Introduced:** Week 9 — Oct 20 · **Due:** Week 10 — Oct 27, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 0%

**Present:** One study sheet with three attractor diagrams, included as page 1 of the 3.5 package; no separate upload or grade.

- Use the same facade, module, view and controlled parameter for all three studies.
- Diagram 1: one point attractor. Diagram 2: multiple point attractors. Diagram 3: one curve attractor.
- Show the attractors and the resulting module variation. Label the parameter and describe how distance changes it.
- For multiple points, state how their influences are combined, such as the nearest point or an average. Show how moving an attractor changes the pattern; no formal equation is required.

<a id="p3c"></a>

### 3.5 — Attractor-based architectural application

**Introduced:** Week 9 — Oct 20 · **Due:** Week 10 — Oct 27, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 10%

**Present:** Two 17 x 11 inch sheets in one PDF: 3.4 studies, then 3.5 elevation/isometric and comparison; editable studies and architectural model.

- Reuse the panel you developed in 3.1 to design a simple facade, wall, canopy, pavilion or similar architectural application. You may develop your 3.2 architectural study further.
- Give the design a clear purpose and scale. Explain what the panel system encloses, screens, shades or defines, and how attractor-driven variation supports that purpose.
- Choose point, multiple-point or curve attractors. You do not need to combine every attractor type in the final design.
- Show one controlled comparison and a resolved elevation and isometric. Identify the attractor, the geometric parameter it drives and why the variation matters architecturally.
- A new precedent study is not required. Facadepot and other references may provide optional inspiration; credit any images or ideas you use.

## P4 — Generative Architectural Envelope

Build a two-parameter field matrix, refine one result into a pavilion or small shop within 12 x 12 x 12 m, then fabricate a contour model.

<a id="p4a"></a>

### 4.1 — Generative fields - a two-parameter matrix

**Introduced:** Week 10 — Oct 27 · **Due:** Week 11 — Nov 3, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 10%

**Present:** One 17 x 11 inch sheet: labeled 5 x 5 matrix, selected result and observations; editable matrix and supplied groups.

- Choose two meaningful parameters, such as texture scale and threshold. Set five distinct values for each.
- Build a 5 x 5 matrix: one parameter changes across columns, the other down rows. Each of the 25 volumes represents one combination. The instructor supplies field tools, not a completed matrix.
- Use the same isometric view, material, lighting and display scale for all cells. Keep other design settings fixed. Label both axes and their five values.
- Mark promising results and briefly explain what each parameter changes and which result you want to develop. Keep the graph editable; do not manually model 25 unrelated objects.
- No separate point-cloud or site-analysis submission is required. You do not need to rebuild the internal SDF tools.

<a id="p4b"></a>

### 4.2 — Architectural envelope - pavilion or small shop

**Introduced:** Week 11 — Nov 3 · **Due:** Week 12 — Nov 10, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 15%

**Present:** One 17 x 11 inch sheet: plan, section, isometric, use/scale and design explanation; editable envelope.

- Choose a pavilion or small shop and state its intended use. Fit the entire envelope within 12 x 12 x 12 meters; these are maximum dimensions, not a required cube.
- Develop the selected field through its controls and necessary openings. Provide a clear entrance, usable occupied space, circulation and a deliberate relationship between ground, enclosure and roof.
- You may also use instructor-provided SDF Boolean operators - union, subtraction and intersection - to combine volumes, carve openings or refine the envelope. Use the operations that help your design; you do not need to use every operator or build the supplied tools yourself.
- Use openings to support access, light or views. Show scale with a person and a few key dimensions.
- Produce one plan, one section and one isometric from the same resolved model. Select drawing locations that explain the interior and its connection to the exterior.
- Focus on a convincing envelope and architectural visualization. Detailed services, full retail planning and construction documentation are outside this exercise. Keep the form suitable for contour fabrication.

<a id="p4c"></a>

### 4.3 — Contour model - registration and assembly

**Introduced:** Week 12 — Nov 10 · **Due:** Week 13 — Nov 17, 11:59 PM Eastern Time · **Weight:** 10%

**Present:** One assembled contour model; one 17 x 11 inch fabrication sheet; separate full-size cutting file, editable source, part list and photographs.

- Use the supplied contouring tools on the 4.2 envelope. Choose one slicing direction and spacing appropriate to the material and form; there is no fixed minimum contour count.
- Use 1:50 as the starting model scale: a 12 m envelope becomes 24 cm. Keep the completed model within the existing 30 cm limit on each axis; review another scale with your professor.
- Number the parts and include a registration mark or feature that establishes their alignment. Hold the model using glue, rods, tabs, spacers, a jig or another simple tested method.
- Test a small group of parts before the full cut. Check material thickness, kerf, alignment and how the assembly preserves openings and spatial qualities.
- Prepare clean full-size cutting curves and a layout within one lab-confirmed sheet of material. Confirm stock and machine access; optional printed components need their own allocation.

## Submission and presentation standards

Use 17 x 11 inch sheets and the Graphic Standards Manual for every assignment. Submit readable PDFs and editable source files, with linked assets packaged and references credited. Keep node names visible and give exposed controls clear names.

Assignment sheets should explain what the system does, which controls matter and why you chose the result. Use ordinary language, diagrams and relevant values; formal equations and mathematical derivations are not required. Teaching presentations may retain their explained mathematics.

Build your own geometry, repetition, conditions, attractor logic and 4.1 matrix. The instructor supplies the generative texture/SDF/volume tools, SDF Boolean operators and contouring groups for Project 4; understand and credit their inputs and outputs rather than rebuilding their internals. A noise-driven volume is not automatically an exact signed distance field.

Open your submission from a clean folder and check the geometry, units and controls. Include the 3.4 study sheet with 3.5. Project 4 has a matrix sheet, an architectural envelope sheet and a fabrication sheet accompanying the physical model.

Submission packaging: each assignment uses a folder named Lastname_Firstname followed by its code: GSM, P2a, P2b, P3a, P3b, P3c, P4a, P4b or P4c. Use the same base name for the presentation PDF. P3c contains both 3.4 and 3.5; do not upload the study sheet twice. Sheet PDFs use 17 x 11 inch landscape pages and the GSM. The 2.2 documentation can reuse existing project pages and has no prescribed page count.

Editable source means the working native file, not just an exported mesh: .blend, or .gh with its referenced .3dm in an approved GH workflow. Keep referenced assets with the source and distinguish the finished result from studies. Fabrication exports supplement the editable source. Package the layout source for the GSM and booklet. Use the announced submission channel; the recorded midterm upload remains Teams. Keep clean folder names if a ZIP upload is required.

Before uploading, open the PDF at actual size, check sheet count and labels, reopen the native file from the submission folder, and confirm that links, units and controls reproduce the work shown. Naming and packaging clarify the current submissions; completed midterm work is not subject to retrospective resubmission.

## Software and data

**The class files are made in Blender Geometry Nodes.** The earlier syllabus also allowed Rhino + Grasshopper; if you already work in an approved environment, you won't have to switch without notice. You don't need to know Python.

For visual work, use Illustrator, Photoshop, InDesign, Inkscape, GIMP, Scribus or a similar vector, raster or layout program. For production, use the slicer and cutting-file workflow the FabLab specifies.

Don't use template-based design tools to make your sheets, Graphic Standards Manual or booklet — the grid, typography, hierarchy and composition are your design work. That rules out Canva, Adobe Express, template-based Figma work, PowerPoint, Google Slides and similar tools.

## Fabrication and materials

Complete the FabLab Safety Orientation and follow the lab's operating requirements. Confirm stock, machine access and production times.

2.2: print the CSG object within 60 mm on each axis and the existing 200 g filament allowance, including failed attempts. Use orientation, splitting or geometry adjustments to avoid or reduce supports. Inspect the layer preview; bridging is acceptable when it works. The recorded midterm upload includes photographs of the print.

4.3: fabricate the 4.2 envelope as numbered contour parts with registration and a tested holding method. The architectural envelope is at most 12 x 12 x 12 m. At 1:50 it is at most 24 cm per axis; the existing physical-model limit remains 30 cm per axis. Use one lab-confirmed material sheet. Test thickness, kerf, alignment and assembly before the full cut. Optional printed components require a separate allocation.

The two physical outcomes are the CSG print and the final contour model. Document tests, failures and revisions; include finished-model photographs in the project documentation.

## AI use in this course

This course teaches node graphs and geometric reasoning. No Python or AI tool-building assignment is required.

**Through Week 10:** you make your own graphs, geometry, layouts and submissions. AI may explain a concept, a piece of syntax or an error message, but it may not write, finish or fix work you submit.

**After Week 10:** you may use AI for code only where an assignment says so. Write your own steps or pseudocode first; then disclose the tool, its version and your prompts, note what you kept or changed, and check the result. This does not replace the required node exercises, and it never allows AI to produce your visual work.

AI image generation, generative fill, AI upscaling, and AI-generated visual identities, palettes or layouts are not allowed in submitted work. You are responsible for everything you submit and must be able to explain and change it. Cite AI use following the University AI policy below.

# Teaching unit outlines

## U01 — Graphic Standards Manual

Set up the graphic system you will use to present all your later work.

**Vocabulary:** composition, grid, hierarchy, typography, line weight, palette.

**Video tutorial:** not yet posted. Use the lesson notes and the class slides.

**Taught in:** [Class 01]({{ site.baseurl }}/modules/classes/class-01/).

1. Compare architectural drawings and identify how hierarchy makes them readable.
2. Study the three manuals below. In each, find one rule, the drawing that shows it at size, and a place where it is applied.
3. Set the page size, margins, columns, type hierarchy, line weights and a restrained color palette.
4. Test the system on a diagram and render, then assemble the four-page manual.

**Practice:** Make a sample 17 × 11 inch sheet and explain one decision about visual hierarchy.

**Use it next:** Apply this system — and keep revising it — in every project and in the final booklet.

**Examples to study:**

- [NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual (1970)](https://archive.org/details/nycta-gs-manual) — Massimo Vignelli and Bob Noorda, Unimark International. A binder of cases: every sign in the New York subway drawn at size with its rule beside it. Full scan.
- [NASA Graphics Standards Manual (1975, NHB 1430-2)](https://archive.org/details/NASA_Graphics_Standards_Manual) — Richard Danne and Bruce Blackburn. One mark, and a hundred pages of where it is allowed to go. What is designed is the consistency. Full scan, public domain.
- [Munich 1972 — visual design guidelines](https://www.otlaicher.de/en/articles/the-rainbow-games/) — Otl Aicher, 1967–1972. A grid, a fixed set of angles and one component varied across a whole field of pictograms. A restricted palette held for four years.

**Read the pseudocode.** Match each step to your nodes; you do not need to type it.

```python
PAGES     = 4                # the whole manual
SHEET     = (17, 11)         # inches
MARGIN    = 0.75
COLUMNS   = 6

TYPEFACES = 2                # 3 is the ceiling
TYPE      = {"title": 24, "heading": 14, "body": 9}
WEIGHTS   = [0.13, 0.35, 0.70]     # thin, medium, heavy
COLORS    = 2                # up to two colors, plus the background
BACKGROUND = "#FFFFFF"       # white or dark
PALETTE   = ["#2455A4", "#E58B32"]  # complementary blue/orange

# every sheet this semester reads these values
```

**Lesson file:** To be prepared and verified.

## U02 — Constructive Solid Geometry

Build solids you can keep editing, using move, rotate, scale and Boolean operations.

**Vocabulary:** parameter, vector, translation, rotation, scale, union, difference, intersection.

**Video tutorials:** [Blender](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HO50aaKbfHY) · [Rhino + Grasshopper](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z0UFlXQnk3g)

**Taught in:** [Class 02]({{ site.baseurl }}/modules/classes/class-02/) · [Class 03]({{ site.baseurl }}/modules/classes/class-03/).

1. Start with one primitive. Find the node's inputs, outputs and parameters.
2. Move, rotate and scale it. Change the order and compare the results.
3. Compare union, intersection and difference. Reverse a subtraction and explain what changes.
4. Expose the useful inputs and build a short massing sequence.
5. In Week 3, check that the CSG object is closed and the right physical size. Export a mesh and, in the FabLab slicer, check the orientation, supports, material use and layer preview.

**Practice:** Draw your CSG steps as a BIG-style process diagram — one operation per frame, read left to right — and change one parameter to show what it does.

**Use it next:** Next, Descriptive Geometry replaces a primitive cutter with a shape you build from points and faces. Week 3 introduces 3D printing: you use units, orientation and slicing to prepare your CSG object for its first print.

**Read the pseudocode.** Match each step to your nodes; you do not need to type it.

```python
# Example sequence; intersection is optional in the assignment.
# Use six to nine frames to explain your own operation sequence.

box     = cube(1.0)                  # 1  primitive
ball    = sphere(r=0.65)             # 2  primitive
rod     = cylinder(r=0.30, h=2.0)    # 3  primitive

ball    = scale(ball, 1.15)          # 4  scale
ball    = translate(ball, z=0.15)    # 5  translate
rod_y   = rotate(rod, x=90)          # 6  rotate - degrees
rod_x   = rotate(rod, y=90)          # 6  same operation

solid   = intersection(box, ball)    # 7  intersection
cutters = union(rod, rod_y, rod_x)   # 8  union
result  = difference(solid, cutters) # 9  difference

# 9 keeps solid, removes cutters. draw 9 again at
# building scale: a figure, planting, ground, shadow.
```

**Teaching note:** In the class file, intersect a cube and sphere, union three perpendicular cylinders, then subtract the cylinders. Parameters remain visible on the native nodes. Join Geometry is an optional comparison, not the final output. For the print, confirm the exported dimensions in the slicer and record the settings and any geometry changes in the P2b submission notes.

## U03 — Descriptive Geometry

Describe geometry as points, lines, edges and faces, then build a solid you control with parameters.

**Vocabulary:** point, vector, parameter, vertex, line, edge, face, mesh, solid, normal.

**Video tutorials:** [Blender](https://youtu.be/JQN7IjVIW4A) · [Rhino + Grasshopper](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g-iOvUYX6Yg)

**Taught in:** [Class 04]({{ site.baseurl }}/modules/classes/class-04/) · [Class 05]({{ site.baseurl }}/modules/classes/class-05/).

1. Point — place a point with X, Y and Z values; tell a position (where something is) from a displacement (how far it moves).
2. Line — connect two positions with a curve.
3. Edge — connect two mesh vertices.
4. Face — put its corners in order and explain which way its normal (its front side) points.
5. Solid — build a pyramid from four base corners and a top point (the apex). Add four side faces and a base, and check that it is closed.
6. Boolean — subtract the pyramid from a cube, revisiting CSG.
7. Panel — define its parameters, calculate the corner points and put the faces in order. Check that it stays closed and tiles across the full range of each parameter.

**Practice:** Keep Width, Depth and Height as exposed inputs. Show the pyramid's five vertices, eight edges and five faces, and subtract it from a cube. Then build your own module and render it with one material you make, on a ground plane, with three-point lighting (key, fill and rim).

**Use it next:** Build the reusable 3.1 module from a documented panel precedent, then use it in the three parts of 3.2.

**Read the pseudocode.** Match each step to your nodes; you do not need to type it.

```python
verts = [[-w, -d, 0],              # 0
         [ w, -d, 0],              # 1
         [ w,  d, 0],              # 2
         [-w,  d, 0],              # 3
         [ 0,  0, h]]              # 4  apex

faces = [[0, 1, 4], [1, 2, 4],
         [2, 3, 4], [3, 0, 4],
         [0, 3, 2, 1]]             # the base — do not forget it

pyramid = mesh(verts, faces)
result  = difference(cube, pyramid)
```

## U04 — Arrays

Arrange your panel with lists, loops and if statements, then carry the same rules into a 3D array.

**Vocabulary:** list, index, count, loop, nested loop, conditional, modulo, sine, amplitude, frequency, phase.

**Video tutorials:** [Blender · Arrays part 1](https://youtu.be/q1z8YI7ExtY) · [Blender · Arrays part 2](https://youtu.be/B7yYA9HCBdM) · [Rhino + Grasshopper · GH list](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ylHphXclA9w) · [Rhino + Grasshopper · Arrays part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ctf8qUgi_ZI) · [Rhino + Grasshopper · Arrays part 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymUSyCUqTL4)

**Taught in:** [Class 06]({{ site.baseurl }}/modules/classes/class-06/). First of two Arrays classes. Build a row, a grid and a layered array with loops and nested loops, then bend the row onto a curve. Name the count, spacing and index in each direction.

**Taught in:** [Class 07]({{ site.baseurl }}/modules/classes/class-07/). Second of two Arrays classes. Patterns start with a brick wall where every other course shifts; then if/Switch rules make façade patterns, and the same rules, reading the layer index, make 3D patterns in an array of cubes. Hexagonal and radial arrays and math-shaped volumes are optional.

1. 1D: build a small row with Repeat Input and Repeat Output. Find the list, the count and the index.
2. 2D: put the row inside a second loop to make a grid. Name the rows and columns, and predict the total count.
3. 3D: stack the grid in layers to make a cube of copies. Before you look, predict how many there are (Count × Count × Count). These are separate copies of one object, not a solid block.
4. Curve: bend the row. Place your module at evenly spaced points along a curve, each turned to follow the curve's direction. The count is the curve's length ÷ the spacing.
5. Pattern example · Brick wall: stack rows of bricks along a curve, one course at a time, and shift every other course by half a brick (k modulo 2). Then swap the curve for a circle.
6. Use Compare and Switch to write if rules; make four different façade patterns by changing selected copies of your panel.
7. 3D patterns: build a 3D array of cubes and let if/Switch rules on the row, column and layer index (i, j, k) drive a parameter — the Switch picks one of two values for size, rotation or height, or keeps or removes the cube. Use the layer index in at least one rule, so the pattern changes from layer to layer as well as across it.
8. Optional practice · Change the cubes' height with a function of X and Y, such as sine or cosine, while keeping the layers in Z (the Sine curve scene).
9. Optional practice · Hexagonal: shift every other row; explain the odd/even test and the row spacing.
10. Optional practice · Radial: place copies around a circle from a radius, a count and an angle step.
11. Optional practice · Drive the curve with a sine wave; explain amplitude (how high), frequency (how often it repeats) and phase (where it starts).

**Practice:** 3.2.1: module and 1D/2D/3D repetition. 3.2.2: four conditional patterns using modulo and an index-driven parameter. 3.2.3: a simple architectural object using those ideas. Submit the three sheets together.

**Use it next:** 3.2.1 repeats the module; 3.2.2 varies it with conditions and indices; 3.2.3 develops a simple architectural object. Mathematical examples explain the operations; equations are not required on the sheets.

**Read the pseudocode.** Match each step to your nodes; you do not need to type it.

```python
# Arrays class 1: line -> grid -> cube -> curve.
row = []
for i in range(nx):
    row.append(place_module(i * dx, 0, 0))

grid = []
for j in range(ny):
    for i in range(nx):
        grid.append(place_module(i * dx, j * dy, 0))

spatial_array = []
for k in range(nz):
    for j in range(ny):
        for i in range(nx):
            spatial_array.append(place_module(i * dx, j * dy, k * dz))

# the row, bent onto a curve: the curve supplies each position
count = int(curve_length(curve) / spacing) + 1
curved_row = []
for i in range(count):
    t = i / (count - 1)                     # 0 at the start, 1 at the end
    p, d = point_on(curve, t), direction_on(curve, t)
    curved_row.append(place_module(p, facing=d))

# Arrays class 2: if / Switch in 2D, then in 3D.
# Sheet 2: one possible facade pattern
for j in range(rows):
    for i in range(cols):
        angle = turn if (i + j) % 2 else 0   # if / Switch
        place_panel(i * dx, j * dy, angle)

# Pattern example: a brick wall, every other course shifted half a brick
for k in range(courses):
    shift = (k % 2) * brick / 2               # 0, 1, 0, 1 ... a rule on the index
    for i in range(count):
        t = i / (count - 1)
        p, d = point_on(curve, t), direction_on(curve, t)
        place_brick(p + d * shift + (0, 0, k * height), facing=d)

# Teaching example: the same rules in 3D. A rule picks one of two values for a parameter
for k in range(layers):
    for j in range(rows):
        for i in range(cols):
            checker = (i + j + k) % 2 == 0          # a 3D checkerboard
            size = big if checker else small        # Switch: two options, one parameter
            turn = 45 if k % 2 else 0               # the layer index drives rotation
            place_cube(i * dx, j * dy, k * dz, size, turn)
```

**Teaching note:** Teach this unit in two classes. Class 1 and its loop tutorial cover explicit repetition, nested loops, indices and counts in 1D, 2D and 3D, then bend the row onto a curve (Part 1 scene 04) — repetition only. Class 2's brick wall (Part 2 scene 08) is the first pattern, where k modulo 2 shifts every other course. The loop pseudocode above is the written tutorial; its Blender recording is linked on the lesson page. Class 2 covers if/Switch in 2D, then the same rules in 3D using the layer index. The Sine curve scene in Arrays Part 2 is optional practice; The 3D conditional examples remain teaching references; the revised third sheet applies the previous work to an architectural object. Distinguish explicit iteration from Blender fields and Grasshopper data trees. A field is not a Repeat Zone.

## U05 — Attractor

Understand fields through one point, multiple points and a curve, then apply the resulting variation to an architectural application.

**Vocabulary:** distance, external condition, field, remap, clamp, falloff, nearest.

**Video tutorial:** not yet posted. Use the lesson notes and the class slides.

**Taught in:** [Class 09]({{ site.baseurl }}/modules/classes/class-09/). October 20: teach the three attractor methods in 3.4 and their architectural application using the existing panel in 3.5. Both sheets are due together October 27.

1. An attractor is a reference in the model. Measure distance from each panel location with Position, Object Info and Vector Math set to Distance.
2. Use Map Range with Clamp to turn distance into scale. Identify the near value, far value and distance limit.
3. For two points, use two Distance nodes and Math set to Minimum; the nearer point controls the response.
4. For a curve, use Object Info, Curve to Mesh without a profile and Geometry Proximity set to Edges. Keep the same Map Range.
5. Test the reusable panel alone, then use For Each Geometry Element to send a different Opening value into its group at each location. Keep the outside dimensions fixed.
6. Replace the sample prefab with the existing student panel, choose a safe parameter range and develop a facade, wall or small architectural project.

**Practice:** Make the three comparable diagrams for 3.4, then use the method of your choice in 3.5.

**Use it next:** 3.4 is a formative study included with 3.5, the architectural application. Combining point and curve attractors is optional.

**Read the pseudocode.** Match each step to your nodes; you do not need to type it.

```python
# Pseudocode: choose ONE of the three distance methods.
for p in panel_locations:
    d = distance(p, point_a)                         # one point
    # d = min(distance(p, point_a), distance(p, point_b))
    # d = distance(p, closest_point(curve, p))

    opening = remap_clamped(d, from_range=(0, 4),
                           to_range=(0.85, 0.15))
    panel = build_panel(opening=opening)  # same prefab, new input
    place(panel, p)
```

**Teaching note:** Start with distance and Map Range; change only the distance source for multiple points and curves. Native node names are retained; explanations belong on Frames. Instance transforms and prefab construction inputs are different responses. Use the small For Each Geometry Element zone only when rebuilding each prefab with its own parameter. Scenes 07-08 repeat the already explained method; they are checkpoints, not additional assignments.

## U07 — Volumetric Data and Fields

Use supplied generative-field tools to explore two parameters systematically and develop a selected architectural envelope.

**Vocabulary:** sample, point cloud, origin, units, decimation, density, voxel, radius, scalar field, implicit surface, signed distance field, isosurface, threshold, noise, resolution.

**Video tutorial:** not yet posted. Use the lesson notes and the class slides.

**Taught in:** Class 10 — *not yet released*. October 27: submit the attractor assignment and begin 4.1. Students build the 5 x 5 matrix using supplied field tools, due November 3. Point-cloud examples are supplementary.

**Taught in:** Class 11 — *not yet released*. November 3: submit 4.1 and develop the 4.2 pavilion or shop envelope using field controls and optional supplied SDF Boolean operators. Plan, section, isometric and source are due November 10.

1. Inspect the supplied texture/SDF tools and identify their controls and outputs.
2. Choose two controls, set five values for each and construct a 5 x 5 matrix.
3. Read the comparison and choose a promising result.
4. Refine it into a small pavilion or shop envelope with usable space and intentional openings.

**Practice:** 4.1: a labeled 25-volume isometric matrix. 4.2: plan, section and isometric of the selected architectural envelope.

**Use it next:** Continue the selected envelope into contour fabrication in 4.3. Point-cloud examples and their mathematical explanations are supplementary, not a separate submission.

**Read the pseudocode.** Match each step to your nodes; you do not need to type it.

```python
cloud = load("site.ply")
print(len(cloud))                          # state this before

cloud = decimate(cloud, keep=0.05)
print(len(cloud))                          # and after

for p in cloud:
    p.density = len(within(cloud, p, radius))

volume = voxelize(cloud, size=0.5)

# A designed field can also define a volume.
def field(p):                              # a shape as a function
    a = sphere_sdf(p, center_a, r_a)
    b = box_sdf(p, center_b, size_b)
    return smooth_min(a, b, k)             # the blend comes free

grid    = sample(field, bounds, resolution)
surface = extract(grid, iso=0.0)           # where the field is zero
```

**Teaching note:** Students build the matrix themselves using earlier repetition skills. Instructors supply the field groups. Keep other settings and display scale fixed while varying the two chosen controls.

## U09 — Discretizing Geometry

Use contours and sections to turn a volume into parts you can fabricate.

**Vocabulary:** section plane, contour, interval, discretization, thickness, registration, kerf, nesting.

**Video tutorial:** not yet posted. Use the lesson notes and the class slides.

**Taught in:** Class 12 — *not yet released*. November 10: submit 4.2 and introduce 4.3 contour fabrication, registration and assembly. Test before the full cut. Bring the completed model November 17 and upload documentation that night. This is the last new required content.

1. Use the supplied contouring group to slice your volume and put the resulting curves in order.
2. Choose one slicing direction and spacing that suit the form, the material thickness and the model scale. Alternatives are shown in class; there is no minimum number of slices and no comparison sheet to submit.
3. Close and clean the profiles you want; turn them into parts with the material's thickness and a clear way to line them up (registration).
4. Test the fit and the kerf, then number, nest and cut the parts, and document the assembly.

**Practice:** Compare the continuous volume, its ordered contours and the assembled parts. Explain what is lost and gained along the way.

**Use it next:** The volume you choose in 4.2 becomes the ordered parts of 4.3 and the laser-cut model of 4.3. Build one fabrication sheet across both stages; printed parts are optional.

**Read the pseudocode.** Match each step to your nodes; you do not need to type it.

```python
sections = []
for k in range(count):
    z = z0 + k * interval
    sections.append(slice(volume, z))      # ordered, and order matters

for i, s in enumerate(sections):
    s = offset(s, kerf / 2)                # the blade has width
    label(s, i)
    nest(s, sheet)
```

**Teaching note:** Designed section parts are distinct from the layers a printer slicer generates. Decide which curves are part boundaries before assigning thickness or sending machine files.

4. After critique, make your chosen revisions. Reuse the sheets that worked and your Graphic Standards Manual; finish the booklet you have built through the semester and check all files.

**Practice:** Bring a fabrication test, a documented revision and a booklet spread for review.

**Use it next:** Submit the booklet, revised manual, editable files and required fabrication work at the final review. Follow the BOOK and 4.3 briefs.

## Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning | Example / distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| parameter | An input you can change that controls a relationship or a result. | Width, Depth and Height on the pyramid. |
| vector | A set of X, Y and Z values that gives a direction and a length (magnitude). The same values can also give a position measured from the origin. | A displacement of (0, 0, 1) moves a point upward one model unit. |
| point | A location in space. | One XYZ position. |
| vertex | A corner point of a mesh; edges and faces are built from these points. | A corner of the pyramid. The plural is vertices. |
| line or curve | A one-dimensional path; the example line joins two positions. | A curve is a different kind of geometry from a mesh edge. |
| edge | A straight connection between two mesh vertices. | One side of a face boundary. |
| face | A mesh surface bounded by vertices and edges, taken in order around its outline. | One triangular side of the pyramid. |
| mesh | Vertices, edges and faces together. A mesh can be open or closed. | Four triangular sides plus a base make the pyramid mesh. |
| solid | A shape that encloses a volume. For the solid exercises its mesh must be closed, with all faces pointing outward. | The capped pyramid before Boolean subtraction. |
| Boolean | Union joins shapes, intersection keeps only where they overlap, and difference cuts one shape out of another. | Cube minus pyramid. |
| list and index | A list is a set of items in order; the index is an item's position in that list. | Array points are numbered from zero. In Blender, a node works on every point at once rather than taking a list as an input. |
| loop | An operation repeated a set number of times; each round can pass its result to the next. | Repeat Input and Repeat Output define a Repeat Zone. |
| nested loop | A repetition inside another repetition. | For every row of a grid, the loop makes all its columns. |
| conditional | A test that chooses a value, or chooses which copies change. | Compare plus Switch; Boolean Math combines tests such as "between two values". |
| field | A value calculated for every point or element — for example, one value per copy in an array. | Distance calculated at every array point; later, a single value measured throughout a volume. |
| attractor | A point, group of points or curve you place in the model; its distance from each element drives a parameter. | Distance rescaled (remapped) into the height of each piece. |
| tessellation and lattice | A tessellation covers a surface with cells; a lattice is a connected network of members in space. | A paneled surface, and a system of nodes and struts. |
| point cloud | A collection of points measured in space, which may also carry data such as color. | Imported site data; keep a record of its source and scale. |
| voxel | One cell of a three-dimensional grid — a 3D pixel. | Smaller cells capture finer detail but take more memory and time to compute. |
| signed distance field | A volume in which every cell stores its distance to the surface, with one sign for inside and the other for outside. | The surface is where the distance is zero. Density or noise values are not automatically distances. |
| discretization | Describing a continuous form with a limited number of samples or parts. | Turning a volume into contour sections, in order, with material thickness. |

## Reading and documentation

No textbook is required. The references below support the lessons; lesson files and tutorials are linked from each class page.

### Reading

- Wassily Kandinsky, Point and Line to Plane — conceptual reference for geometry and graphic relationships.
- Robert Woodbury, Elements of Parametric Design — relationships, dependencies and change.
- Casey Reas, Chandler McWilliams and LUST, Form+Code — repetition, transformation and visualization.
- Arturo Tedeschi, AAD Algorithms-Aided Design — an additional Grasshopper reference where that environment is supported.
- Diego García Cuevas and Gianluca Pugliese, Advanced 3D Printing with Grasshopper: Clay and FDM — fabrication and toolpath reference.
- Anthony Di Mari and Nora Yoo, Operative Design: A Catalog of Spatial Verbs — the CSG operations named as spatial acts; primary reference for the massing sequence.
- Anthony Di Mari, Conditional Design: An Introduction to Elemental Architecture — the companion volume; operations driven by a condition or rule.
- Neil Spiller, Drawing Architecture; Peter Cook, Drawing: The Motive Force of Architecture — architectural drawing and visual communication.

### Example graphic standards manuals

Shown in Class 01 and the reference for the Graphic Standards Manual. Each is a page grid, a type hierarchy and a rule for every case that comes up. Read them for how much of each one is rules rather than pictures.

| Manual | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| [NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual (1970)](https://archive.org/details/nycta-gs-manual) | Massimo Vignelli and Bob Noorda, Unimark International. A binder of cases: every sign in the New York subway drawn at size with its rule beside it. Full scan. |
| [NASA Graphics Standards Manual (1975, NHB 1430-2)](https://archive.org/details/NASA_Graphics_Standards_Manual) | Richard Danne and Bruce Blackburn. One mark, and a hundred pages of where it is allowed to go. What is designed is the consistency. Full scan, public domain. |
| [Munich 1972 — visual design guidelines](https://www.otlaicher.de/en/articles/the-rainbow-games/) | Otl Aicher, 1967–1972. A grid, a fixed set of angles and one component varied across a whole field of pictograms. A restricted palette held for four years. |

### Visual precedents

| Reference | Use |
| --- | --- |
| [@mmnksr](https://www.instagram.com/mmnksr/) | Point-cloud and section imagery; compare representation choices. |
| [@mantissa.xyz](https://www.instagram.com/mantissa.xyz/) | A second point-cloud/section reference for visual comparison. |
| [@saul_kim_](https://www.instagram.com/saul_kim_/) | Composition, restraint and spatial legibility. |
| [@facadepot](https://www.instagram.com/facadepot/) | Components, façades and controlled variation. |

### Technical documentation

- [BIG-style process diagram tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Y5Rn3bDL5s) — CSG 2.1: reference for the operation sequence and graphic presentation.
- [Three-point lighting tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RDbrOpnIY7Q) — Module 3.1: reference for one consistent key, fill and rim/back lighting strategy across three panel variations.
- [Blender Repeat Zone](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/5.2/modeling/geometry_nodes/utilities/repeat_zone.html) — Explicit iteration with Repeat Input and Repeat Output.
- [Blender Field to Grid](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/5.2/modeling/geometry_nodes/volume/operations/field_to_grid.html) — Sampling fields on a voxel-grid topology.
- [Blender SDF Grid Offset](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/5.2/modeling/geometry_nodes/volume/operations/sdf_grid_offset.html) — Distance-based offset of an SDF surface.
- [Blender 5.2 manual](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/5.2/index.html) — Check exact node behavior against the version used to prepare the lesson.

## Artificial Intelligence Preamble

FAU recognizes the value of generative AI in facilitating learning. However, output generated by artificial intelligence (AI) — written words, computations, code, artwork, images, music, and so on — is drawn from previously published materials and is not your own original work.

FAU students are not permitted to use AI for any course work unless explicitly allowed to do so by the instructor of the class for a specific assignment. [Policy 12.16 Artificial Intelligence]

Class policies related to AI use are decided by the individual faculty. Some faculty may permit the use of AI in some assignments but not others, and some faculty may prohibit the use of AI in their course entirely. In the case that an instructor permits the use of AI for some assignments, the assignment instructions will indicate when and how the use of AI is permitted in that specific assignment. It is the student's responsibility to comply with the instructor's expectations for each assignment in each course. When AI is authorized, the student is also responsible and accountable for the content of the work. AI may generate inaccurate, false, or exaggerated information. Users should approach any generated content with skepticism and review any information generated by AI before using generated content as-is.

If you are unclear about whether or not the use of AI is permitted, ask your instructor before starting the assignment.

Failure to comply with the requirements related to the use of AI may constitute a violation of the Florida Atlantic Code of Academic Integrity, Regulation 4.001.

**Proper Citation:** If the use of AI is permitted for a specific assignment, then use of the AI tool must be properly documented and cited. For more information on how to properly cite the use of AI tools, visit https://fau.edu/ai/citation

## Attendance Policy Statement

Students are expected to attend all their scheduled University classes and to satisfy all academic objectives as outlined by the instructor. The effect of absences upon grades is determined by the instructor, and the University reserves the right to deal at any time with individual cases of non-attendance. Students are responsible for arranging to make up work missed because of legitimate class absence, such as illness, family emergencies, military obligation, court-imposed legal obligations, or participation in University-approved activities. Examples of University-approved reasons for absences include participating on an athletic or scholastic team, musical and theatrical performances, and debate activities. It is the student's responsibility to give the instructor notice prior to any anticipated absences and within a reasonable amount of time after an unanticipated absence, ordinarily by the next scheduled class meeting. Instructors must allow each student who is absent for a University-approved reason the opportunity to make up work missed without any reduction in the student's final course grade as a direct result of such absence.

### Course-Specific Attendance Terms

This course meets **once per week**. A single absence is roughly seven percent of the semester's contact time, and each session contains material that is not repeated.

- Attendance and participation constitute **5% of the final grade.** Each unexcused absence reduces this component by one third; each unexcused late arrival (more than 15 minutes after the start of class) reduces it by one sixth.
- Students absent more than **three** classes without serious documented reason, given in writing in advance where possible, may — at the instructor's judgment — fail the course.
- Students absent from a required pin-up, review, or submission receive an F for that assignment.
- Absence does not extend a deadline. It is the student's responsibility to obtain material covered and to submit work due.

Attendance is recorded through a sign-in link provided at the start of each session. `[CONFIRM whether Google Form or Canvas attendance is used this term]`

### Classroom Etiquette

Personal communication devices should not be used for non-course purposes during class. Devices are permitted for documentation, reference, and coursework. Students not participating in class may be considered absent at the discretion of the instructor.

---

## Policy on Make-up Tests, Late Work, and Incompletes

Absence does not absolve the student from homework, assignments, or work progress due on the day of absence, or work due the following class. In case of absence, it is the student's responsibility to obtain information on material covered and assignments.

**Late work is not accepted.** Missed projects or class activities resulting from an unexcused absence receive a zero.

**Revision.** This course is built on iteration, and revision is handled through a defined mechanism rather than through late submission. Assignment grades are issued at the original deadline and stand. All work may be revised for inclusion in the Final Booklet, where the quality of that revision is assessed as 40% of the Booklet grade. Students who submit nothing at the original deadline have nothing to revise.

Incompletes are granted only under University policy and only where the majority of coursework has been completed.

---

## Project Documentation of Student Work

The School of Architecture reserves the right to retain all student work for the purpose of record, exhibition, and instruction. All students are encouraged to reproduce all work for their own records prior to submission of originals to the instructor. In the event of publication, the author of the work will be recognized and receive full attribution. Upon completion of the final review, all students are required to submit any requested revisions and all digital material from the whole semester through a shared Google Drive, Microsoft Teams, or other online platform specified by the instructor. **Final grades will be withheld until this material is turned in.**

## Code of Academic Integrity

Students at Florida Atlantic University are expected to maintain the highest ethical standards. Academic dishonesty is considered a serious breach of these ethical standards, because it interferes with the university mission to provide a high quality education in which no student enjoys an unfair advantage over any other. Academic dishonesty is also destructive of the university community, which is grounded in a system of mutual trust and places high value on personal integrity and individual responsibility. Harsh penalties are associated with academic dishonesty. For more information, see University Regulation 4.001.

---

## Faculty Rights and Responsibilities

Florida Atlantic University respects the rights of instructors to teach and students to learn. Maintenance of these rights requires classroom conditions that do not impede their exercise. To ensure these rights, faculty members have the prerogative to:

- Establish and implement academic standards.
- Establish and enforce reasonable behavior standards in each class.
- Recommend disciplinary action for students whose behavior may be judged as disruptive under the Student Code of Conduct, University Regulation 4.007.

---

## Disability Policy

In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act Amendments Act (ADAAA), students who require reasonable accommodations due to a disability to properly execute coursework must register with Student Accessibility Services (SAS) and follow all SAS procedures. SAS has offices across three of FAU's campuses — Boca Raton, Davie and Jupiter — however disability services are available for students on all campuses. For more information, please visit the SAS website at www.fau.edu/sas/.

---

## Religious Accommodation Policy Statement

In accordance with the rules of the Florida Board of Education and Florida law, students have the right to reasonable accommodations from the University in order to observe religious practices and beliefs regarding admissions, registration, class attendance, and the scheduling of examinations and work assignments. University Regulation 2.007, Religious Observances, sets forth this policy for FAU and may be accessed on the FAU website at www.fau.edu/regulations.

Any student who feels aggrieved regarding religious accommodations may present a grievance to the executive director of The Office of Civil Rights and Title IX. Any such grievances will follow Florida Atlantic University's established grievance procedure regarding alleged discrimination.

## Time Commitment Per Credit Hour

For traditionally delivered courses, not less than one (1) hour of classroom or direct faculty instruction each week for fifteen (15) weeks per Fall or Spring semester, and a minimum of two (2) hours of out-of-class student work for each credit hour. Equivalent time and effort are required for Summer Semesters, which usually have a shortened timeframe. Fully Online courses, hybrid, shortened, intensive format courses, and other non-traditional modes of delivery will demonstrate equivalent time and effort.

---

## Grade Appeal Process

You may request a review of the final course grade when you believe that one of the following conditions apply:

- There was a computational or recording error in the grading.
- The grading process used non-academic criteria.
- There was a gross violation of the instructor's own grading system.

University Regulation 4.002 contains information on the grade appeals process.

---

## Policy on the Recording of Lectures

Students enrolled in this course may record video or audio of class lectures for their own personal educational use. A class lecture is defined as a formal or methodical oral presentation as part of a university course intended to present information or teach students about a particular subject. Recording class activities other than class lectures, including but not limited to student presentations (whether individually or as part of a group), class discussion (except when incidental to and incorporated within a class lecture), labs, clinical presentations such as patient history, academic exercises involving student participation, test or examination administrations, field trips, and private conversations between students in the class or between a student and the lecturer, is prohibited. Recordings may not be used as a substitute for class participation or class attendance and may not be published or shared without the written consent of the faculty member. Failure to adhere to these requirements may constitute a violation of the University's Student Code of Conduct and/or the Code of Academic Integrity.

While the University is sensitive to the financial and professional needs of our students, outside employment is not considered an extenuating circumstance in cases of poor performance, excessive absences, or failure to submit assigned work on schedule.
